# Follow-Up to AI SOC Automation Claims: Validating the 8x Detection Speed Improvement

**Problem:** Agentic SOC platforms claim 8x faster detection. These claims are vendor-reported and not independently validated. Understanding whether the improvement persists on diverse incident types is a natural follow-up.

**Direction:** Use a public SOC simulation dataset (e.g., DARPA Transparent Computing, CICIDS2017) to compare time-to-detection between: (a) rule-based baseline, (b) LLM-assisted triage. Measure time-to-correct-escalation for three incident types (intrusion, malware, phishing). Compute speedup ratios per incident type.

**Why it matters:** Vendor-reported speedup claims need independent validation. If speedup is incident-type-dependent, relying on AI for all SOC workflows may miss certain threat classes.

**Relevant context:** AI SOC Automation guide 2026 (UnderDefense): 8x detection speedup claim. CICIDS2017 and similar public SOC datasets are accessible. Independent validation of AI SOC performance not found in peer-reviewed literature.

# Follow-Up to LLM-Enhanced Fuzzing: Does AI Seed Generation Actually Improve Coverage on Security-Critical Paths?

**Problem:** LLM-enhanced fuzzing (PromeFuzz, ChatAFL) shows coverage improvements in general. It is not established whether these improvements specifically cover security-critical code paths (not just coverage in general).

**Direction:** Run standard AFL++ and LLM-enhanced fuzzing (using a GPT-4o-guided seed generator) on 5 open-source C libraries with known CVEs. Measure: (a) general code coverage, (b) coverage of security-critical paths (identified by security annotations or manual review), (c) vulnerability detection rate. Compare security-critical coverage vs. general coverage improvement.

**Why it matters:** Higher general coverage may not translate to better vulnerability discovery if AI seeds avoid security-critical paths. This follow-up would reveal whether LLM-fuzzing improves security outcomes specifically.

**Relevant context:** PromeFuzz: 1.5x-3.88x branch coverage improvement (ACM CCS 2025). ChatAFL: 5.8-6.7% code coverage improvement (NDSS). Neither measures security-critical path coverage specifically.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Requirement Elicitation for Open Source Projects

**Problem:** Open-source projects often lack explicit security requirements. Vulnerabilities may reflect missing requirements as much as implementation errors. AI could assist in eliciting implicit security requirements from code and documentation.

**Direction:** For 10 open-source projects with known CVEs, use an LLM to infer implicit security requirements from source code, documentation, and commit history. Compare inferred requirements to requirements explicitly violated by each CVE. Measure: what fraction of CVEs reflect requirement violations that the AI could have predicted?

**Why it matters:** Proactive security requirement elicitation could prevent vulnerabilities before implementation, not just detect them after. This is a novel upstream defense.

**Relevant context:** FormaliSE 2026 covers AI in formal requirements. Security requirement elicitation using LLMs is not a studied application area despite clear feasibility.

# Novel Direction: Differential Security Analysis Using Multiple AI Models as a Team

**Problem:** Individual AI models have consistent blind spots. Using multiple models and comparing their findings could identify vulnerabilities that any single model misses.

**Direction:** Run three AI models (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) independently on 20 vulnerable code samples. Compute: agreement rate, disagreement patterns, and whether the union of all three models' findings covers more vulnerabilities than any individual model. Measure the marginal detection gain from adding each model.

**Why it matters:** If models have complementary blind spots, ensemble approaches could dramatically improve defensive coverage. This is an actionable insight for deployers.

**Relevant context:** Ensemble methods in ML are well-established. Multi-model security analysis as a deliberate defensive strategy has not been studied. Published AI vulnerability detection research uses single models.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Debt Quantification

**Problem:** Technical debt is a software engineering concept for deferred maintenance. Security debt — accumulated vulnerabilities and weaknesses not yet addressed — lacks a quantitative measure. AI could enable automated security debt scoring.

**Direction:** Define a security debt metric: weighted sum of (vulnerability severity × age × exploitability × patch availability). Use an LLM to compute this metric for 10 open-source projects. Validate by correlating security debt score with subsequent breach/CVE history. Compute inter-rater reliability of AI-generated scores.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying security debt enables prioritization and resource allocation. AI-automated security debt scoring could provide a continuous signal for maintainers.

**Relevant context:** Technical debt quantification is a studied SE research area. Security-specific debt quantification using AI is novel. CVSS scoring provides component inputs but not a debt score.

# Novel Direction: Measuring AI Defensive Capability as a Function of Adversary Sophistication

**Problem:** AI defense tools are typically evaluated against known vulnerabilities. Their performance against adversarially obfuscated code, or against novel attack patterns specifically designed to evade them, is not characterized.

**Direction:** Design a red-team experiment: have one AI model (attacker) generate obfuscated versions of vulnerable code designed to evade detection. Have another AI model (defender) attempt to detect the obfuscated vulnerabilities. Measure detection rate degradation vs. non-obfuscated baseline. Iterate for two obfuscation levels.

**Why it matters:** In practice, sophisticated attackers will attempt to evade AI defenses. This experiment characterizes the robustness of AI defense under adversarial conditions.

**Relevant context:** Adversarial evasion of malware detectors is well-studied. Adversarial evasion of static vulnerability scanners by code obfuscation has not been systematically studied for LLM-based scanners.

# Causal Chain: Intervening on the Human Expertise Bottleneck in AI-Assisted Vulnerability Verification

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners generate findings, but verification requires expert judgment. The causal chain: AI finds vuln → expert verifies → patch deployed. The verification bottleneck slows remediation.

**Direction:** Design a tiered verification protocol: (a) AI-only verification (LLM checks its own finding), (b) non-expert CS student verification with AI guidance, (c) expert verification. Run all three on 15 findings. Measure: verification accuracy, time, and cost per tier. Identify the minimum verification tier that achieves acceptable accuracy.

**Why it matters:** If non-experts with AI guidance can accurately verify findings, the verification bottleneck can be broken without expensive expert time. This changes the economics of AI-assisted defense.

**Relevant context:** Qualys Agent Val addresses validation. DARPA AIxCC: $152/task average. Expert verification bottleneck not characterized as a causal link in remediation pipelines.

# Compounding Risk: AI Overconfidence + Missing Ground Truth = Undetectable Performance Degradation

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: (1) AI security tools may be overconfident in their outputs (poor calibration); (2) defenders often lack ground truth to verify AI performance in production. The combination means performance can degrade undetected.

**Direction:** Design a monitoring protocol for AI security tool performance without ground truth: use proxy metrics (finding rate stability, explanation consistency across runs, agreement with independent re-analysis). Test the protocol on a simulated degradation scenario (vary model version or prompt). Measure whether the proxy metrics detect performance degradation.

**Why it matters:** Production AI defense tools with no monitoring mechanism may degrade silently. This is a safety-critical governance gap.

**Relevant context:** AI monitoring in production is a general ML ops challenge. Security-specific monitoring without ground truth is novel. Temperature/consistency experiments (see earlier ideas) provide methodological groundwork.

# Calibration Study: Do AI Security Confidence Scores Reflect Actual Exploitability?

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners produce confidence scores for their findings, but it is not known whether these scores correlate with actual exploitability (CVSSv3 exploitability subscore).

**Direction:** Run an AI vulnerability scanner on 40 CVEs with known CVSSv3 exploitability scores. Measure Spearman correlation between AI confidence score and CVSSv3 exploitability. Compute calibration curve. Test whether high-confidence AI findings are disproportionately high-exploitability.

**Why it matters:** Well-calibrated confidence scores enable rational prioritization. If AI is overconfident on low-exploitability findings and underconfident on high-exploitability ones, defenders are misinformed.

**Relevant context:** CVSSv3 exploitability metrics are published for most CVEs in NVD. AI scanner confidence calibration to exploitability not studied in the literature.
